title: Conformity assessment procedures under the AI Act
explain_beginner: This paper looks at how high-risk AI systems are checked for safety and compliance under the AI Act. The authors map which checking procedure applies to which kind of AI system, so it is clearer which route a given system must follow. They find that the law borrows procedures from older European rules that were not designed with AI in mind. Because of this, the risk categories may miss dangers that are specific to AI, and some procedures may not really fit AI systems. The work matters because it points out gaps that regulators and companies need to address.
explain_business: For executives, this paper clarifies which conformity assessment route a high-risk AI system will take under the AI Act, and warns that the rules lean on older European procedures not built for AI. In practice, the risk categories may not capture AI-specific dangers, and the chosen procedure affects what conformity assessment bodies must do. This informs decisions about compliance planning, budgeting, and which notified body or internal process to use. It also signals where regulatory expectations may shift, so leaders can build flexibility into product timelines and risk management rather than assuming current classifications are final.
explain_practitioner: The authors analyse conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems under the AI Act. They first map the applicable procedures to different system types, providing structured implementation guidance. They then assess the Act's reliance on procedures from other Union harmonisation legislation, showing that this borrowing produces a risk classification that underweights AI-specific risks and questioning whether the procedures suit AI systems. They also examine how assigning these procedures shapes the obligations of conformity assessment bodies. The key contribution is a systematic analysis of the regulatory landscape that exposes systemic challenges and regulatory blind spots.
